title: Before the Hot Big Bang: Cosmic Inflation vs. Bouncing & Ekpyrotic Cosmology — The CMB horizon, flatness, and magnetic monopole crises; Alexei Starobinsky's 1980 R + R^2 plateau & Alan Guth's 1981 false-vacuum inflation; Planck 2018's 8-sigma scalar red tilt (n_s = 0.9649) & BICEP/Keck's 2021 r < 0.036 execution of chaotic monomial potentials; Khoury, Ovrut, Steinhardt & Turok's 2001 ultra-stiff ekpyrotic slow contraction, Brandenberger & Vafa's 1989 blue-tensor string-gas Hagedorn phase & Ijjas, Steinhardt & Loeb's 2013-2014 eternal-inflation multiverse critique; 60-e-fold flatness, slow-roll (n_s, r), ekpyrotic BKL suppression & LiteBIRD/CMB-S4 math plus spotting early-universe assumptions in disguise

teenKit.tldr: Opposite sides of the universe share an identical temperature despite being too far apart to ever communicate, forcing physicists to debate whether the early cosmos underwent a massive expansion spurt called inflation or an alternative bounce.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how the universe coordinated its temperature in its infancy reveals how space itself can stretch faster than light, setting the stage for every star, planet, and living thing to exist today.
keyTakeaways: The Cosmic Microwave Background is the ancient, 13.8-billion-year-old afterglow of the universe, boasting a remarkably uniform temperature across opposite sides of the sky.
Cosmic inflation solves the horizon and flatness problems by proposing that the early universe experienced a sudden, exponential burst of rapid expansion.

Rival theories like ekpyrotic cosmology and string-gas models challenge inflation, arguing the universe may have bounced or contracted before expanding instead of starting with a standard big bang singularity.

vocab.meaning: The leftover thermal radiation from the early universe, captured as an ancient snapshot of the cosmos when it first became transparent.
The maximum distance that light or any physical signal could possibly have traveled since the beginning of the universe.
A theory stating that the early universe underwent a brief period of hyper-fast exponential expansion, smoothing out its geometry and temperature.
A rival model to inflation where the universe begins with a slow contraction and bounces back instead of expanding from an infinitely dense singularity.

quiz.question: What major puzzle is created when scientists measure the temperature of the Cosmic Microwave Background on opposite sides of the sky?
options: The universe is spinning too fast for gravity to hold galaxies together.
Distant patches of the sky share the exact same temperature despite being too far apart to ever exchange information.
The universe contains too many magnetic monopoles to allow stars to form.
Light travels slower today than it did 13.8 billion years ago.
quiz.explanation: Opposite sides of the observable universe are separated by dozens of causal horizons, meaning they never had time to communicate or equalize their temperatures naturally.

quiz.question: How did Alan Guth and Alexei Starobinsky's theories of inflation solve the horizon problem?
options: By proposing that light used to travel a million times faster than it does now.
By suggesting the universe is actually shaped like a giant donut.
By forcing a tiny, locally connected patch of space to rapidly expand into the massive universe we see today.
By proving that temperature variations do not actually exist in deep space.
quiz.explanation: Inflation takes a tiny region of space where temperatures had plenty of time to equalize and blows it up faster than light, carrying those identical temperatures across the entire cosmos.

quiz.question: What is the core premise of the ekpyrotic model championed by Paul Steinhardt and his collaborators?
options: The universe started from an infinitely hot singularity and expanded once.
The universe goes through cycles of slow contraction followed by a non-singular bounce rather than a standard big bang.
Space is entirely flat because of microscopic strings vibrating in eleven dimensions.
Dark energy will eventually slow down and cause the universe to collapse forever.
quiz.explanation: Ekpyrotic cosmology replaces the big bang singularity with an ultra-stiff period of slow contraction that ends in a smooth, cosmic bounce.
